title: Implement tasks that promote reasoning & problem solving
subtitle: Choose tasks worth thinking about — open enough that students have to reason, not just recall a procedure you already showed them.

sections.sources: Source: NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) · Stein & Smith, Mathematical Tasks Framework · Adding It Up (2001).

blocks.text: Effective teaching engages students in solving and discussing tasks that promote reasoning and problem solving — tasks with multiple entry points and varied solution strategies.

The task is the single biggest lever a teacher pulls. A task of **high cognitive demand** asks students to make sense of relationships, choose a path, and justify it. A low-demand task asks them to repeat a procedure. The trap is that a rich task can quietly become a low one: the moment we pre-teach the exact steps or narrow it to one “right” method, the reasoning evaporates and we’re back to follow-along.
What it looks like in grades 6–8

items: Tasks with a **low floor and high ceiling** — everyone can start, and there’s somewhere for everyone to go.
More than one valid strategy, so a real discussion is possible.
Students decide *how* to approach it; the teacher hasn’t already modeled the answer.
Struggle is expected and planned for, not rescued away with hints at the first sign of it.

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: Students choosing strategies and defending them
Several different approaches on the walls
“I’m not sure yet, but I tried…”
The teacher maintaining demand instead of over-scaffolding

no.title: We should *not* see
items: “Do it the way I just showed you”
One-step recall dressed up as a “problem”
Hints that hand over the thinking at the first pause

blocks.text: Where it lives in our toolbelt

This practice is the heart of [Rich Tasks / Three-Act Math](/math/approach/rich-tasks) and [Thin-Slicing](/math/approach/thin-slicing). Running tasks on [vertical surfaces with random groups](/math/approach/vnps) keeps the demand high, and the [5 Practices](/math/approach/five-practices) are how you orchestrate the reasoning a good task produces.
Take a procedure you were going to demonstrate and instead pose it as a question first: “How could we figure this out?” You’ve just raised the cognitive demand without finding a new task.
